summary: Proposes an ietf URN namespace for naming IETF documents, including RFCs, STDs, FYIs and BCPs, and the minutes of working group and BOF meetings.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2648 proposes a URN namespace for RFCs and other IETF documents, Internet Drafts, and meeting minutes. A name keeps identifying the same resource even if the document changes, while a resolver can help locate a copy.

questions: what is the ietf urn namespace
how do i write a urn for an rfc
subtitle: The ietf URN namespace gives IETF documents and meeting records persistent names.

tldr.problem: The URN framework needs to support new naming systems, including a namespace for IETF documents and meeting records.
tldr.mechanism: The memo proposes the formal namespace identifier ietf and defines forms for RFCs, other document series, Internet Drafts, meeting minutes, and future extensions.
tldr.outcome: An assigned URN is never reassigned to another resource, even if the document changes. RFC 2648 is Informational and has been updated by RFC 6924 and RFC 9141.

today: RFC 2648 is Informational and has been updated by RFC 6924 and RFC 9141. Read those updates with it for the later definition of the ietf namespace.

sections.title: A URN Namespace for IETF Records
sections.content:
RFC 2648 proposes the formal URN namespace ietf. It covers RFC-family documents published by the RFC Editor, IETF working-group and birds-of-a-feather meeting minutes, and Internet Drafts published by the Internet Drafts Editor.

The proposal gives a naming structure for these records. It does not make the URN a location: a resolver needs access to a mirrored copy of the underlying documents to provide a citation or a location.
sections.plainLanguage: The namespace gives IETF documents and meeting records a structured name. The name identifies a record; a separate resolver can help find a copy of it.

sections.title: How an ietf URN Is Written
sections.content:
The namespace-specific part follows urn:ietf:. Document-series names use prefixes such as rfc:, fyi:, std:, and bcp:, followed by digits. Internet Draft names use id:, and meeting names use mtg:, each followed by a string made from letters, digits, or hyphens.

The grammar also reserves room for another prefix for future expansion. The entire URN is case-insensitive. The RFC warns that the grammar may need an update if a new document series or other characters are introduced.
sections.plainLanguage: An ietf URN starts with urn:ietf: and then identifies a document series, draft, or meeting record. Capital letters do not change the name.

sections.title: Unique and Persistent Assignments
sections.content:
The RFC Editor's index files are the definitive assignment records for RFCs, STDs, FYIs, and BCPs. Meeting URNs include the IETF conference sequence number, and the Internet Drafts Editor's index is definitive for draft names.

Once assigned, a URN is never reassigned to a different resource. That rule is separate from whether the underlying document can change: the RFC Editor may update a document or a series may consist of a changing set of RFCs. New names are assigned when a document is published, meeting minutes are filed, or an Internet Draft is published.
sections.plainLanguage: Official indexes determine which names have been assigned. A name is never given to a different resource, even if the document or collection it identifies later changes.

sections.title: Resolving a Name to a Document
sections.content:
The memo requires a mirrored copy of the underlying documents for resolution. Its appendix gives example scripts that can turn a URN into a citation, a URL, a list of URLs, another URN, or the resource itself. The examples look up document numbers in index files and meeting names in a conference table.

The scripts return an error for an unrecognized name or one that cannot be found. They are examples of resolution for the proposed namespace, not a promise that every name has a working copy at every location.
sections.plainLanguage: A resolver checks the name against document indexes and meeting records. It can then return information or a location for a matching record, or an error if it cannot find one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The namespace adds no reserved characters beyond those in the general URN syntax, and its namespace-specific strings do not use those reserved characters. The RFC says that a resolver must report incorrect syntax when characters in the string have been escaped.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposed names use a limited character set. A resolver must reject a name with invalid escaping rather than treat it as a valid name.
